content: 1. Lebina et al. (2018) conducted a study on the PrePex circumcision device, focusing on adverse events and the use of analgesia during device removal. Their findings were published in PLoS One. 2. Tshimanga et al. (2016) evaluated the safety profile of the PrePex male circumcision device and client satisfaction among adolescent males aged 13–17 years in Zimbabwe. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 3. Mavhu et al. (2019) investigated whether the PrePex device could serve as an alternative to surgical male circumcision for adolescents aged 13–17 years. Their findings, based on routine service delivery and active surveillance in Zimbabwe, were published in PLoS One. 4. Tshimanga et al. (2016) conducted a Phase II randomized controlled trial comparing the safety, procedure time, and cost of the PrePex device to forceps-guided surgical circumcision in Zimbabwe. The results were published in PLoS One. 5. Bochner et al. (2017) analyzed the adverse event profile of a mature voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) program in Zimbabwe, which utilized both PrePex and surgical procedures. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 6. Galukande et al. (2017) conducted a cohort study in Uganda to assess long-term outcomes following PrePex male circumcision in an urban population. The study was published in BMC Research Notes. 7. Odoyo-June et al. (2016) reported unexpected complications following adult medical male circumcision using the PrePex device. Their findings were published in Urologia Internationalis. 8. A GRADE evidence profile was developed to address whether surgical assist devices could be used as an alternative to surgery for men aged 15–49 years seeking circumcision for HIV prevention. The evidence was assessed in low-resource settings, with a focus on safety, acceptability, and outcomes. 9. Millard et al. (2014) conducted a study in South Africa on the UniCirc™ v2 device, evaluating adverse events, procedure time, pain, intra-operative blood loss, wound healing, and cosmetic results. The study also tested a modified version of the device in 50 clients. 10. Millard et al. (2015) performed a cohort study in South Africa to assess the eligibility, adverse events, procedure time, wound healing, satisfaction, and cosmetic outcomes of the UniCirc™ v2 device. Topical anesthesia with a lidocaine/prilocaine mixture was used prior to circumcision. 11. Millard et al. (2014) conducted a randomized trial of the UniCirc device, a novel disposable tool for rapid, minimally invasive adult voluntary male circumcision. The study was published in the South African Medical Journal. 12. Millard and Goldstuck (2015) carried out a multi-center field trial on no-needle, single-visit adult male circumcision using the UniCirc device. The findings were published in PLoS One. 13. Shenje and Millard (2016) conducted a randomized field trial on sutureless adult voluntary male circumcision using the UniCirc device with topical anesthetic. The study was published in PLoS One. 14. Millard (2019) explored the use of the UniCirc device for circumcision in adolescent boys aged 12–15 years in a study registered under NCT02593630. 15. Evidence-to-decision frameworks were developed to evaluate the use of device-based methods for circumcision, including collar clamps, elastic collar compression devices, and surgical assist devices. The quality of evidence was moderate for males aged 15 years and older but low for those aged 10–14 years. 16. Device-based circumcision methods were found to have similar efficacy to surgical methods in achieving successful circumcision. However, one device type was associated with higher rates of tetanus, a rare but serious complication. 17. Device-based circumcision methods generally had high satisfaction rates among adult men and adolescent boys, with minimal interference in daily activities. However, healing times were longer compared to surgical methods, requiring extended abstinence from sexual activity. 18. Procedure times for device-based circumcision were shorter than those for surgical methods, but the costs of devices and associated medical supplies were notable contributors to overall expenses. 19. Evidence on the impact of device-based circumcision on health equity and implementation feasibility remains limited. However, these methods have been shown to allow less surgically skilled providers to perform the procedure effectively.
